Salesforge Whitelabel is the only reseller platform that lets you rebrand a full multichannel outreach product (cold email and LinkedIn) with no cap on mailboxes or LinkedIn accounts per client subscription, all sitting under your own custom domain.
Your clients log in at app.youragency.com, see your logo, your color scheme, your support email, and the pricing plans you set. Salesforge is invisible to them.

Your clients can run cold email steps and LinkedIn steps inside the same campaign, with real if-this-then-that logic. If a connection request is accepted, the sequence sends a LinkedIn message. If not, it falls back to email.

Sales consultants and agencies whose clients run cold outreach at real volume (thousands of emails a week, dozens of mailboxes) and need dedicated email infrastructure resold under their own brand.

Shared email infrastructure is fine until one sender in the pool starts blasting spam, gets the IP flagged, and drags every other sender's deliverability down. Dedicated IPs mean each of your clients gets their own IP address to build a sender reputation on, and their own IP address to protect.

So, if your clients are running 20+ mailboxes across multiple domains and sending thousands of emails a week, that kind of client is where Infraforge fits, and where your reseller economics actually work.

Every mailbox runs on a dedicated IP address that belongs to your client alone. Nobody else's sending behavior can affect their inbox placement. For high-volume clients, you can assign multiple IPs and split their campaigns across them, so a heavy cold outreach push does not hurt the deliverability of their transactional emails.

Every domain you register gets SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configured automatically. These are the email authentication records inbox providers like Gmail and Outlook check to confirm a sender is not spoofing someone else's domain. You skip the manual DNS work, and there is no waiting on propagation troubleshooting when you onboard a new client.

You see every client's email across every mailbox they run, in one dashboard. If you manage 5 clients each running 20 mailboxes, that is 100 mailboxes to check on manually. Masterbox collapses all of them into a single view so you spot issues in seconds instead of hours.

They pack a lot into one product, and that is exactly why it works as a white label SaaS platform: a CRM, a funnel and landing page builder, email and SMS campaigns, a calendar tool, forms, membership sites, and review management.

On top of that, the base plan is only part of the bill. Every email your clients send, every SMS they blast, every AI token they use, and every phone minute they burn is billed as usage on top of your subscription. This can still be attractive for small businesses served by agencies, since it bundles several functions into one branded system.
Multichannel (email, SMS, and voice calls):

Your clients can send email campaigns, blast SMS, and even make phone calls from one account. This is why the platform reads as a real marketing tool to a client, not just another CRM. Heads up: email, SMS, and phone minutes are all billed as usage on top of your base plan.

Your clients set up flows like "new lead comes in, wait 5 minutes, send an email, if they do not reply in 24 hours send an SMS, if they book a meeting notify the sales rep." These automation tools support broader marketing strategies, not just one-off workflows. This is the feature I hear most agencies use to prove ROI to their clients at renewal time.

In SaaS Mode, you decide the markup on GoHighLevel's usage charges (email, SMS, AI, phone) and bill your clients at your marked-up rate. Every SMS blast your client sends can generate margin for you on top of their subscription while supporting recurring marketing campaigns and ongoing marketing efforts. Small numbers, but they add up when you have 30 clients running SMS campaigns every month.
Combines CRM, funnels, email, SMS, calendars, memberships, and more in one platform, reducing the need for additional software

The label gets stretched. Some programs sold as white-label only swap a logo, while the vendor's name still shows in the dashboard, the billing, or the support emails. A real one means the client logs in on your domain, is billed by you, and does not need to know who built the software.
Your logo and colours on a Trillet-hosted address on Studio; your own domain, branded email, and minute markup on Agency. Not a wrapper.
In a real one, the client logs in on your domain, is billed by you, and does not need to see the vendor. If the vendor's name still shows in the dashboard, the emails, or the invoice, it is a badge.
Branding depth matters because client trust breaks when dashboards, emails, or reports show the vendor name.

Ask how much branding you really get in custom white label solutions. Can you use your logo, your domain, your email templates, and your report style. Can you change packages for different niches. Flexibility helps you sell to more industries without rewriting everything.

Yes, white label services are legal in most cases. It is a common model in software, marketing, and eCommerce. The key is the contract. Your reseller agreement should clearly cover licensing, branding rights, data handling, and who owns what. Also check if any industry rules apply, like email outreach compliance or ad platform policies, because those are separate from “white label” itself.

Every white-label reseller program sells the same promise: your brand on the software, strong margins, recurring revenue, live by the weekend. I believed that promise too, back when I ran my own agency, before I joined Trillet. The promise is easy to make. The real difference sits underneath it, in the part you only meet once a client is live under your name.
What is a white-label reseller program?

A white-label reseller program lets you sell a vendor's product under your own brand. You buy access at a wholesale rate, put your name and domain on it, set the retail price, and own the client relationship. The vendor stays invisible and runs the platform. You keep the margin for as long as the client stays.

It is worth separating from the deals vendors often lump in with it. A reseller sells the vendor's product for a cut, often with that brand still visible. A referral partner passes leads for a fee and does not deliver the service. An OEM embeds the vendor's technology inside its own product. White-label sits closest to owning the offer the client sees.
Your brand, domain, and retail price on the vendor's product

The label gets stretched. Some programs sold as white-label only swap a logo, while the vendor's name still shows in the dashboard, the billing, or the support emails. A real one means the client logs in on your domain, is billed by you, and does not need to know who built the software.
